title: Wildlife fell 73% on average since 1970, which is not the same as losing 73% of animals
body: In October 2026, WWF's Living Planet Report found that monitored populations of wild vertebrates fell by an average of 73% between 1970 and 2022, across 35,803 populations of 5,790 species. The figure is the Living Planet Index, kept by the Zoological Society of London: it averages how much each population changed relative to its own size, so a big population counts no more than a small one, and it says nothing directly about how many animals were lost or how many species died out. In the index makers' own example, populations of 400, 50 and 33 become 420, 20 and 33: the average change is −18%, yet only 2% of the animals are gone. About half the populations are stable or rising; the index falls because the declines are deeper and because species-rich groups, such as amphibians and reptiles in Latin America, count for more ([technical report](https://osf.io/wravx/overview)). Freshwater populations fell most, by 85% on average.

slides.question: Three populations of 400, 50 and 33 animals become 420, 20 and 33. What share of all the animals is lost?
slides.explanation: Only 10 of 483 animals, about 2%, even though the three populations changed by −18% on average. The Living Planet Index follows the average change, not the head count.

slides.alt: Animation in dusk-forest greens: a bar falls 73% from 1970 to 2022. Dot clusters stand for populations; three of 400, 50 and 33 animals change by +5%, −60% and 0%: −18% on average, 2% of animals lost. Then a doubling and a halving cancel, half the populations rise, and bars by habitat and region.

slides.prompt: Change three populations of 400, 50 and 33 animals. Make an index like the Living Planet Index fall by half while the number of animals doesn't drop.
slides.takeaway: Let the big population grow a little and crash the two small ones: the index plunges while the total holds. It follows each population's change, not the head count.

slides.heading: How much monitored populations fell on average, 1970–2022
slides.note: Living Planet Report 2026, by WWF and the Zoological Society of London

slides.heading: About half of the monitored populations are stable or rising
slides.note: 43.1% rising, 6.9% stable and 50.0% falling over the years each was counted

slides.heading: Then why does the index fall?
slides.text: The falls are deeper than the rises. The index also weights each group of species by how many species it holds, so species-rich groups, such as amphibians and reptiles in Latin America and fish in Africa, where many populations fall steeply, count for more. And it adds up the changes year by year since 1970.

slides.question: What does the 73% fall in monitored wildlife since 1970 measure?
options: The share of all wild animals lost
The share of species gone extinct
slides.explanation: The Living Planet Index averages how much each monitored population changed relative to its own size. It is not a head count, and it doesn't count extinctions.
